1163.title: Controversy
1163.hook: in the 1230s some banned and burned his books
1163.howItsDone: Printed editions of the Mishneh Torah carry commentaries around the text, including the Rabad's critical notes, so disagreement is part of the page students study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Guide's last page: know God's ways, then walk in them, with kindness, justice and righteousness. Your line: knowledge leads to kindness. Today, the fights over the man who wrote it.

Open a printed Mishneh Torah to a page of its Book of Knowledge and look at the margins. Next to Maimonides' clean Hebrew sit other voices, in smaller type. Some explain him. Some defend him. A few say, more or less, he's wrong. The book that became a pillar of Jewish learning started out in a fight. In his own lifetime people accused him. After his death, some rabbis banned his philosophical writings, and accounts tell of copies being burned.
screen: `VOICES IN THE MARGIN.` → `ACCUSED, THEN BANNED.` → `WHAT CAME OUT THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: Controversy. First, the accusation. While Maimonides was alive, some readers said his code barely spoke about the resurrection of the dead, and wondered whether he believed in it. He answered with a whole essay: yes, he did, and it already stood in his own list of principles. A man known for clarity had to explain himself. Second, the critic in the margin. A scholar in Provence, Rabbi Abraham ben David, known as the Rabad, wrote sharp notes on the code. Where Maimonides calls anyone who imagines God with a body a heretic, the Rabad objects: greater and better people than that, he writes, held such a view, misled by the plain words of verses. He isn't saying God has a body. He's saying don't call sincere people heretics. Those notes are printed right beside the code. Third, the fire. After Maimonides died, a bitter dispute broke out over his philosophy. Some rabbis feared the Guide and the Book of Knowledge would lead readers away from simple faith, and banned their study. Others defended him just as fiercely. Accounts say his books were burned; historians still argue over exactly who did what. Fourth, then canon. An argument for the sake of heaven, says the Mishnah, will endure, like the arguments of Hillel and Shammai. The banned books stayed on the shelf. His principles went into the prayer book. The critic and the criticized now share a page. Controversy didn't erase him. It became part of how he is read.

Next to it, find one thing that person saw clearly, one sentence of credit. Then picture the two of you on a single page, your note in the margin beside their words, both kept.
Controversy. In Hebrew, machloket. For Maimonides it meant accusation, critique and even burned books, and then a place at the center of Jewish learning. Today's word.

1164.title: Nachmanides' other way
1164.hook: a more mystical approach to the same texts
1164.howItsDone: The Ramban's Torah commentary is printed in standard rabbinic Bibles, and students often read it alongside other commentators, comparing how each one reads the same verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, controversy: Maimonides accused, critiqued in the margin, banned, and then read at the center. Your line: controversy, then canon. Today, a rival who argued with him by name.

A hot afternoon. Abraham sits at the opening of his tent, looks up, and sees three men standing nearby. He runs to meet them, bows, and hurries Sarah to bake bread while he picks out a calf. A homely scene from Genesis. Now hand it to two great rabbis named Moses. One says it all happened in a prophetic vision. The other says those words contradict Scripture. Same text, same tent, two very different readings.
screen: `THREE MEN AT THE TENT.` → `A VISION?` → `OR SOMETHING ELSE?`

segments.voice: Nachmanides' other way. His name was Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, known as the Ramban, from Girona, in Catalonia. First, he argues out loud. In the Guide, Maimonides reads the three men as something Abraham saw in a prophetic vision. In his commentary on Genesis, the Ramban quotes him, then pushes back hard: these words, he says, contradict Scripture, and one shouldn't listen to them. If it was only a vision, why the bread, the calf, the hurrying? He reads the visitors as real messengers, seen in a form people could see. Second, the offerings. Maimonides explains the sacrifices as a gentle step: people in the ancient world knew worship by offerings, so the Torah kept the form and turned it toward God alone. The Ramban objects. The Torah calls an offering "of a sweet savour unto the LORD." He sees in it a picture for the one who brings it: what is done to the animal should make the person think, this should have been me, and the offering stands in their place. Third, the way of truth. The Ramban drops a short hint and says the meaning is known by the way of truth, pointing to a hidden, mystical layer of the Torah, the tradition known as Kabbalah. He hints. He doesn't spell it out. Fourth, two ways, one Torah. Maimonides reaches for reason and philosophy; the Ramban, for the plain story and for hidden depths. Both read the same verses seriously. Students still open both, side by side, and learn from the argument.
screen: `HE ARGUES OUT LOUD.` · `A SWEET SAVOUR UNTO THE LORD.` · `THE WAY OF TRUTH.` · `TWO WAYS, ONE TORAH.` · then, large: `TWO WAYS OF THINKING.`

segments.voice: Pick one question that matters to you, like why people suffer or why pray, and give it two readers: one who answers with careful reasons, step by step, and one who answers with a story, or a sense that something deeper is hidden there. 1165.title: His son Abraham
1165.hook: Abraham Maimonides wrote of intense inner devotion
1165.howItsDone: Jewish prayer asks for kavanah, intention, and some people slow down at key lines, such as the first verse of the Shema, to say them with full attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ramban read the same verses as Maimonides and argued, toward the plain story and a hidden depth. Your line: two ways of thinking. Today, the son who came after.

The child of a famous parent hears one question again and again: are you going to be just like your father? Maimonides had a son named Abraham. He inherited his father's books, his father's critics, and, tradition says, his father's role leading the Jews of Egypt. But when Abraham sat down to write his own great book, it wasn't another law code, and it wasn't another Guide. It was about the inside of a person at prayer.
screen: `JUST LIKE YOUR FATHER?` → `THE BOOKS, THE CRITICS, THE ROLE.` → `HIS OWN BOOK.`

segments.voice: His son Abraham. First, the father's line. In his law code, Maimonides wrote that prayer without kavanah, without intention, is not prayer. A person should clear the mind, he says, and see themselves as standing before God. A law, stated in a sentence. Second, the son's book. Abraham Maimonides wrote a large work in Judeo-Arabic, its title often given as a complete guide for the servants of God. It turns that sentence about intention into a whole way of life: humility, generosity, patience, solitude, nights awake in prayer. He calls it a path, and the people walking it he calls hasidim, the devoted. Third, the neighbors he noticed. Abraham lived among Muslims and saw the discipline of the Sufi mystics. He wrote that some of their practices looked like what the ancient prophets of Israel once did, practices he felt his own people had lost. So he urged praying with the whole body: bowing low, kneeling, standing in ordered rows, raising the hands. Some in his community pushed back, and the argument was real. Fourth, a line from the Psalms that puts this kind of devotion in a few words: "I have set the LORD always before me." The father gave reasons for faith and a code for living it. The son asked what it feels like from inside, when a person actually means the words. Both are Maimonides. One wrote the law of intention. The other tried to live inside it.

1166.title: Reading him honestly
1166.hook: some of his views reflect his time, and later readers wrestle with them openly
1166.howItsDone: Jewish study often reads a classic text together with later commentators who question it, so disagreement with a great teacher is part of learning him, and different communities handle hard passages in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abraham Maimonides took his father's law of intention and built a whole path of devotion on it. Your line: the son's path. Today, how to read the father when a page hurts.

A treasured book, a beloved teacher, and then a page that stops the reader cold: a line about who can learn, or who matters, that lands badly today. There are a few easy ways out. Rip out the page. Pretend you never saw it. Or throw away the whole book. Readers of Maimonides meet pages like that. And the surprising thing is that Maimonides himself handed them a better way to handle it.
screen: `A PAGE THAT STOPS YOU COLD.` → `RIP IT, HIDE IT, OR TOSS IT?` → `A BETTER WAY.`

segments.voice: Reading him honestly. First, his own rule. In the introduction to his Eight Chapters, Maimonides says he drew on the words of sages and of philosophers, and that a person should accept the truth from whoever says it. Truth isn't weighed by the name on it. Second, he did this to the sages. In the Guide he takes up the astronomy found in the Talmud, where some details don't fit what was known in his day. Don't be troubled, he says: the sages' astronomy came from the science of their own time, not from prophecy. He honored them, and still said where their knowledge was of its age. Third, a page of his own. In his laws of Torah study, Maimonides writes that a woman who studies Torah receives a reward. Then he adds that the sages commanded a father not to teach his daughter Torah, and gives a reason about women's minds that some readers today find painful. There are other passages too, about other peoples, that some readers wince at. Fourth, wrestling in the open. Later readers haven't hidden these lines. Some read them narrowly, as limited to one kind of study. Some say, as he said of the sages, that here he spoke from his own time. Some simply disagree with him. Today girls and women study Torah in communities across the Jewish world, and they read Maimonides too. Reading him honestly means keeping the whole page in view: the brilliance and the blind spot, side by side, with no need to tear either one out.

1167.title: The physician's prayer
1167.hook: a famous prayer for physicians is attributed to him, though probably written later
1167.howItsDone: Jews pray for the sick in synagogue with a blessing called the Mi Sheberach and in the daily Amidah's blessing for healing, and some medical ceremonies read the physician's prayer, often still under Maimonides' name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reading him honestly: the brilliance and the blind spot, kept on the same page. Your line: read with honesty. Today, a prayer that carries his name.

A framed page hangs on the wall of a doctor's office. A prayer in a physician's voice, asking for love of the work and patience with the sick, and at the bottom, a name: Maimonides. It fits. He was a doctor at court in Cairo. He wrote medical books. Who else would it be? And yet the trail of that prayer leads somewhere else.
screen: `A FRAMED PRAYER.` → `SIGNED: MAIMONIDES.` → `WHOSE IS IT REALLY?`

segments.voice: The physician's prayer. First, what it asks. In it a doctor asks God for love of the art and of every creature, for a mind clear at the bedside, and to be kept from greed and the hunger for fame. And it asks that the doctor see in the sick person only a fellow human being in pain. Second, where it comes from. The prayer isn't found in Maimonides' own writings. It appears in print long after his death, in German, and the scholars who have traced it point to a later physician, often named as Marcus Herz. Third, what Maimonides did write about healing. In his commentary on the Mishnah, he treats healing as a duty drawn from the Torah's law of lost property: the command to return what your neighbor has lost, he says, includes helping return a person's lost health. And the Torah itself names God as healer: "for I am the LORD that healeth thee." Fourth, attributed, not his. The rabbis cared about who said what. The Talmud teaches that whoever repeats a saying in the name of the one who said it brings redemption to the world. So a careful reader can still love this prayer, hang it on the wall and say it, with its true label on it.

1168.title: Tiberias
1168.hook: he is buried in Tiberias, visited by many
1168.howItsDone: Jews visit the graves of family and of great teachers to pray and recite psalms, often leaving a small stone, and add 'may his memory be a blessing' when speaking of someone who has died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prayer for doctors that carries Maimonides' name, though scholars trace it to a later hand. Your line: attributed, not his. Today, the place where tradition says he rests.

A lake in the north of the land of Israel, the Sea of Galilee, with a city on its western shore. Fishing boats, a promenade, hot springs, heat that hangs over the water in summer. And a short walk up from the shore, a tomb where people stop to pray, light candles and leave small stones. Maimonides died in Egypt. Yet this is where tradition says he rests.
screen: `A CITY ON THE SEA OF GALILEE.` → `CANDLES AND SMALL STONES.` → `WHY HERE?`

segments.voice: Tiberias. First, the journey. Maimonides died in Egypt, where he had worked as a doctor and led a community. Tradition says his body was carried from there to the land of Israel and buried in Tiberias, and legends grew up around that journey. Some readers see a wish behind it: to lie in the land whose laws fill so much of his code. Second, the stone over him. You met his epitaph early in this block: from Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses. Tradition links that saying to his grave, and places other great teachers buried nearby, so a walk through that part of the city passes through generations of learning. Third, what people do there. They come to pray, to recite psalms, to light a candle. Some leave a small stone on the grave. The reasons people give vary: a sign that someone visited, a marker that lasts longer than flowers, a way of saying the memory still stands. Jewish teachers who speak about prayer at a grave often stress that the prayer is directed to God, sometimes asking for help in the merit of the righteous person buried there. Fourth, the blessing in a name. Proverbs says, "The memory of the righteous shall be for a blessing." That verse stands behind the words said after the name of someone who has died: zichrono livrachah, may his memory be a blessing. And so his name, too, is said with a blessing after it.
screen: `FROM EGYPT TO THE LAND OF ISRAEL.` · `FROM MOSES TO MOSES.` · `PSALMS, CANDLES, A SMALL STONE.` · `MAY HIS MEMORY BE A BLESSING.` · then, large: `RESTING IN TIBERIAS.`

If a loss ever feels too heavy to carry alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

1169.title: Thought and deed
1169.hook: his legacy joins philosophy and law
1169.howItsDone: Jewish learning pairs study with practice: people study the laws of Shabbat, prayer or giving and then keep them, and some study Maimonides' code and his Guide side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tiberias: a tomb by the Sea of Galilee, candles, small stones, and a name said with a blessing. Your line: resting in tiberias. Today, the two halves of his legacy.

Two books on one shelf. One is thick with rules: how to pray, how to give, how to keep Shabbat, how a court works, what to eat. The other is full of questions: what words about God can mean, why the commandments exist, how a mind draws near to God. The same man wrote both. You could treat them as two different authors, the lawyer and the philosopher. But look at how each one begins and ends, and the two start to reach for each other.
screen: `A BOOK OF RULES.` → `A BOOK OF QUESTIONS.` → `ONE AUTHOR.`

segments.voice: Thought and deed. First, the code starts with thought. Before a single rule about food or Shabbat, the Mishneh Torah opens with knowing that there is a first Being, and with love and awe of God. The law book stands on a foundation of thinking. Second, the Guide ends with deed. You heard it last week: the book of philosophy closes with Jeremiah, and with going out to do kindness, justice and righteousness. Third, an old argument. The Talmud tells of sages gathered in an upper room in Lod, asking which is greater, study or deed. Rabbi Tarfon said deed. Rabbi Akiva said study. And they all answered together: study is greater, because study leads to deed. Study wins by pointing past itself. Fourth, the other side of the scale. In Pirkei Avot, Shimon, the son of Rabban Gamliel, says that study isn't the main thing; the deed is. Read together, the two sayings hold each other in place. Thought without deed goes nowhere. Deed without thought can go anywhere. That's the shape of Maimonides' legacy: the philosopher wrote law, the lawgiver wrote philosophy, and each was meant to lead into the other. It's the shape of this week too: an argument in the margin, a rival reading, a son's prayer, an honest page, a prayer's true label, a grave by the water. Each one was a thought someone carried out into the world.
screen: `THE CODE STARTS WITH THOUGHT.` · `THE GUIDE ENDS WITH DEED.` · `STUDY LEADS TO DEED.` · `THE DEED IS THE MAIN THING.` · then, large: `THOUGHT AND DEED.`

segments.voice: Choose one idea from this week that stayed with you: credit before criticism, a second reader, saying a line slowly, an honest label, a teacher's name. Hold it for a few breaths, then picture one small act this thought would actually do, and let the thought and the act sit together, joined.
Thought and deed. Maimonides' legacy: law that begins with knowing God, and philosophy that ends in kindness, each leading into the other. Today's word.
